Metaprogramming attributes can be generalized into a hierarchical programming syntax.

## Example

```js
- =on
  - keyDown
    - meta
    - shift
    - d
  - =>
    - =subCategorize
    - =type
      - Done
```

→ 

```js
// thoughts that start with = are interpreted as metaprogramming attributes as usual
// ineffectual in themselves but available for evaluation with the right user interaction
on({
  // non-leaf thoughts interpreted as objects
  keyDown: [
    // leaves in object property position interpreted as array items
    'meta', 
    'shift', 
    'd'
  ], 
  // lambda function given a generated key when expected to be an object property
  __lambda__0: () => {
    // lambda children interpreted as function body
    subCategorizeOne()
    // leaves of function interpreted as position arguments
    type('Done')
  }
})
```

Which would move a thought into a Done category when executed:

```js
- To Do
  - Code Reviews
```

→ 

```js
- To Do
  - Done
    - Code Reviews
```

## Attributes

Attributes can be fully evaluated during rendering.

For example, instead of a simple scalar value:

```js
- =note
  - hello em
```

A note could contain a dynamic expression:

```js
- =note
  - =date
    - mm/d/yyyy // formats today's date
```

Or query other thoughts:

```js
- =note
  - =concat
    - hello
    - /Friends/*[1]
```

which would evaluate to something like this:

```js
'hello' + query('/Friends/*[1]')
```

Setting the note to 'hello' plus the value of the first thought in `/Friends`.
input.title: Generalize metaprogramming

Crop all the empty space above and below the visible content when autofocus is active. Cropping needs to occur seamlessly and maintain the perceived scroll position. 

Consider the following approaches:

1. ~Shift the content and adjust the scroll position by the same amount.~
   - ✗ Risk of jitter
   - Autofocus *usually* only occurs when navigating, not when scrolling. 
   - However it is possible to navigate and then scroll before the autohide animation completes.
   - Probably best to crop before the animation completes. 
   - Bottom is easier than top since the footer is kept below the fold. 
   - What about autoscroll on new subthought? 
   - **✗ Safari mobile screen flash during CSS transition**
2. Shift the toolbar and footer and block scrolling above and below.
   - ✗ Scroll bar position will be wrong.
   - ✗ Lose native scroll bounce.
   - ✗ Risk of autoscroll breakage.
3. ~~Re-render at top/bottom as soon as empty space is exhausted.~~
   - **✗ Flash will still occur since navigating to parent requires repositioning.**
	- ✗ Scroll bar position will be wrong until end is reached.
	- Possibly preserves native scroll bounce (?)
4. Software scroll
   - ✗ Non-native performance
      - Even very careful software scroll does not feel right 
      - https://idiotwu.github.io/smooth-scrollbar/
   - Requires custom spring implementation
5. Scroll mirroring
   - Steps
     - Set Content to position: fixed
     - Set height of body to height of Content
     - On scroll, translate Content by the same amount.
   - ✓ Correct scroll bar position
   - ✓ No flash, since content is always in the viewport
   - ✓ Preserves native scroll bounce*
     - ✗ *Possible lag
- `overscroll-behavior: contain`
   - Steps
     - Instead of scrolling the body, scroll a container element that only includes the visible thoughts. 
   - ✓ Correct scroll bar position
   - Can thoughts be moved in and out of the container without interrupting their animations?
     - i.e. simultaneous scroll and fade [thoughts] and pan [content]
     - Scroll + Fade
       - Multigesture stops scroll, so there can be no momentum scrolling on mobile while a gesture is performed. 
       - Back button can be hit on desktop during fade though. 
     - Fade + Scroll
       - Easily reproduced on both platforms with cursorUp/Down then scroll. 
   - May be combined with scroll mirroring to avoid having to actually contain the thoughts. 

![image](https://github.com/cybersemics/em/assets/750276/f6051261-0f8e-429d-ae26-23d340d17e14)
input.title: Crop empty space around autohide

1 `rem` equals the font size of the root element (`<html>`).
1 `em` equals the element's inherited font size (thus is sensitive to all ancestor's `fontSize`).

Currently, `em` is used to scale elements across the app according to `state.fontSize`, which is a user font size setting. This includes the size of buttons, panels, toolbar, icons, etc, not just font size. User controlled font size is critical for both user preference and low vision users, and mobile users do not have convenience of <kbd>Command/Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>+</kbd>. 

The use of `em` is made possible by [setting fontSize on the Content container](https://github.com/cybersemics/em/blob/7a1af9934377f3c5bd5bd68f73dc5d7947a80b4e/src/components/AppComponent.tsx#L197). However, `em` units are affected by the font size of all ancestors, which is usually not the intention. This really should have used `rem` all along. Regrettably, there are places where the desired font size *depends* on the inheritance feature, so this is not a trivial change.

Refactor `em` to `rem` and fix any visual regressions.
input.title: Migrate `em` to `rem` css units

> Now that the second stage's fundamental mechanics have been implemented in #3439, replace `CommandTable` with a new component designed and implemented specifically for the Command Center's second stage. ## Links - [Figma design](https://www.figma.com/design/oQnevfxv79fhTJnOs0fz9k/em-design?node-id=6025-69973&t=wcIvhH5h9raLRj64-4) ## Background In #3439 we implemented the core mechanics of the second stage drawer – the snap point, gestural mechanics, and so on. We used the existing `CommandTable` as a stopgap. It validated the general concepts and allowed focus to remain on fundamental mechanics. But this component isn't suitable long-term: - **Outdated design** – reflects the old design language, not the liminal UI direction we've been building towards - **Accumulated complexity** – over time, `CommandTable` has been used in more and more contexts, resulting in complex logic, branching conditions, and props that make it difficult to extend - **Regression risk** – further expanding it risks breaking existing code that relies on it For these reasons, in this issue we'll design and implement a new component from scratch, specifically for the Command Center's second stage drawer. ## Paired commands One key difference between `CommandTable` and this new implementation is that some commands will be displayed in **two columns** rather than just one. You can see an example of this in the screenshot at the top of this issue. See how Move Up and Move Down split into **two columns** rather than the single column that most commands occupy. This represents **paired, or grouped, commands**. Many commands in **em** have inverse or related operations. For simplicity's sake, we now join these together on one row. Perhaps there could be a simple property in the `Command` interface that specifies which commands are paired with which. **These commands should be paired for now, as a proof of concept**. There are perhaps more commands we could pair, but this will get us started: - `cursorNext` & `cursorPrev` - `jumpBack` & `jumpForward` - `moveCursorBackward` & `moveCursorForward` - `moveThoughtUp` & `moveThoughtDown` - `undo` & `redo` ## Aesthetics & visual deconstruction This section breaks down the visual components of the new design. If you need any more details, please let me know. It's okay (and I actually generally *encourage*) eyeballing font sizes and margins, as long as it looks coherent, good values are used (e.g. use `rem`, use clear divisions like 0.25, 0.5, 1, use unit-based spacing) A link to the full design in Figma is also available at the top of this issue for your reference. ### Command glow - Each command in the expanded view has a **background glow**. - The screenshot above isolates the command glows, so you can see the impact they have. - You can see these directly in Figma [via this link](https://www.figma.com/design/oQnevfxv79fhTJnOs0fz9k/em-design?node-id=7844-117612&t=wcIvhH5h9raLRj64-4). - These use `mix-blend-mode` to modulate the Command Center's **background glow** with each command's background glow – approximating the way colour and light blend in the real world. - There are **two instances of the glow** for each visible command stacked on top of each other. - One uses `saturation` at `50%` opacity, a blur radius `96px`, and fill `linear-gradient(95deg, rgba(220, 220, 220, 0.51) 16.97%, rgba(238, 238, 238, 0.17) 93.52%)`. - One uses `plus-lighter` at `50%` opacity, a blur radius `96px`, and fill `linear-gradient(95deg, #FF6565 16.97%, rgba(232, 232, 232, 0.33) 93.52%)`. - IIRC this is the same technique used to implement the active button glow in the Command Center's standard view. - Stacking them together like this has a kind of additive effect – we boost the saturation of the Command Center's background glow, and increase its luminosity. - There are two variants of this background glow: one for **one-column commands (wide)** and one for **two-column commands (narrow)**. Both are essentially the same, just different dimensions. The glow should cover the entire region of their associated command. - _Exact_ visual parity with Figma is not _necessarily_ required – so long as the layered glow effect, blend modes, and relative intensity feel correct. Eyeballing is actually encouraged! Use judgment to make sure the end result feels close to the design. > **Note**: I know we've had issues integrating `mix-blend-mode` in the past, especially when it intersects with other backdrop filters, blurs, and animations – and I'm also aware this issue leans more heavily on these properties than the other pieces of work you've taken on. > If we _do_ run into recurring issues like we have in the past, I'm open to reworking certain design elements if it proves too difficult/impossible to mitigate those issues, or if performance issues become a concern. > Let's give it a go in its maximal form first, and we'll scale back or optimize if it feels necessary. ### Command group header background (separator) - There's a _very subtle_ dark blurry line underneath each command group header, which we use as a visual **separator.** - The screenshot above isolates the separator, so you can see its impact. It's subtle. It's designed to create a boundary in the "light field", and help mitigate the command glows overly blending with one another. - This is a simple **thick black line**, 48px blur radius, with fill/stroke color `rgba(14, 10, 32, 0.63)`. - It uses `mix-blend-mode` `plus-darker` at `7%` opacity. - For resizing/responsiveness, we should use `background-position: center`, and not scale the line to fit the screen's width – rather, just reveal more of it. The initial scale of the line image can be tweaked based on what feels faithful to the mockup. ### Grid of commands - The grid of commands itself is pretty straightforward. - It's divided into command groups, with about 4/4.5 `rem` worth of margin between groups. - The main change is the command pairing – sometimes commands taking one column and sometimes taking two. ### Command interactions - On tap, the command should be executed, and the entire command (its glow, and its contents) should fade out to 60% opacity using duration `fast`. On release, all elements should come back up to 100% opacity. - Unavailable commands should appear at 35% opacity. ### Section headers - These use 50% gray (`gray50`) and `mix-blend-mode` `plus-lighter`, at `100% opacity`. ## Other details - **Component naming**: open to whatever feels reasonable – not necessarily committed to "command table" if it feels like there's a better fit. - Search and sort are **not in scope for this issue** – they will be addressed later on. For now, it's okay to mark this issue as complete without search. ---

Acceptance criteria

 - [ ] New component replaces `CommandTable` in Command Center's second stage - [ ] Commands render in groups with ~4-4.5rem margin between groups **Paired commands** - [ ] The following commands display in two columns on one row: - `cursorNext` & `cursorPrev` - `jumpBack` & `jumpForward` - `moveCursorBackward` & `moveCursorForward` - `moveThoughtUp` & `moveThoughtDown` - `undo` & `redo` - [ ] All other commands display in a single column **Command glow** - [ ] Each command has two stacked glow layers behind it - [ ] Layer 1: `mix-blend-mode: saturation`, 50% opacity, 96px blur - [ ] Layer 2: `mix-blend-mode: plus-lighter`, 50% opacity, 96px blur - [ ] Wide variant for single-column commands, narrow variant for paired commands - [ ] Glow covers entire command region **Separator** - [ ] Dark blurry line appears under each command group header - [ ] Uses `mix-blend-mode: plus-darker` at 7% opacity, 48px blur - [ ] Horizontally centered, does not scale to fit width **Section headers** - [ ] Use `gray50` with `mix-blend-mode: plus-lighter` at 100% opacity **Interaction states** - [ ] On tap: command executes, fades to 60% opacity (duration `fast`) - [ ] On release: returns to 100% opacity - [ ] Unavailable commands display at 35% opacity

**Portals** are how we distinguish **transcluded** views from "normal" views in **em**. The mockups here show what portals should look like on desktop and mobile. **This asset will be needed for development:** [portal.avif](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26640519/portal.avif.zip) ## Terminology - **Normal view**: **em**'s normal hierarchical view – a literal representation of the thought tree. - **Transcluded view**: A subset of thoughts from elsewhere in the hierarchy transposed into the current view. Examples include **Context View** and **Transcluded Search (WIP)**. - **Portal parent**: The thought that opens the portal (e.g. the thought on which Context View is toggled). In the mockup, **"Virgil Abloh"** is the portal parent. - **Portal children**: The transcluded thoughts rendered within the portal. ## Architecture Right now, Context View is the only transcluded view in **em**, so test with this during development. The portal's root element should be implemented as a **single absolutely-positioned `
`** inside `LayoutTree`'s inner container – the same container that holds all thought nodes. By living inside the existing layout container, the portal inherits existing transforms (autocrop, indent animations, autofocus) for free. This absolutely positioned portal div should be a sibling of `BulletCursorOverlay` and the `TransitionGroup` of thought nodes, rendered before them so it sits behind the content (`z-index: -1`). ## Composition A portal is composed of two simple layers: ### 1. Color blend A simple image that produces the portal's spectral hue effect. - **Implementation**: A nested inner `
` within the portal container, with the image as its `background-image`. This inner div is the only element that moves during parallax and autofocus — via `transform: translate(x, y)`. Decoupling the image from the mask allows each to be positioned and animated independently. - **Dimensions**: The image spreads across the entire screen width and should be **1.5×–2× the viewport height**. The oversized height prepares us for parallax shifting effects. - **Position**: Controlled by `transform` on the inner div. This is GPU-composited (no paint, no layout recalc) and allows us to implement transitions and animations on the portal independent of the `LayoutTree`. - **Image**: portal.avif (linked as an asset). ### 2. Mask — Portal Region Constrains the color blend to the visible region on-screen that contains portalled thoughts, with soft feathered edges (vignette). - **Implementation**: A `mask-composite` approach that separately masks the top/bottom and right-hand edges. A reference image at the top of the page shows the target appearance — match it visually. - **Bounding box**: Derived from `treeThoughtsPositioned`: - **Top edge**: The portal parent's `y` position (the thought that opened context view). - **Bottom edge**: `max(y + height)` across all portal children. - **Vertical padding**: Tuned by eye to give the feathered edges room to breathe. Match the reference image. - **Horizontal extent**: The portal div should use a large negative `left` and oversized `width` (e.g. `left: -50vw`, `width: 200vw`) to guarantee the background reaches the left edge of the viewport regardless of the parent container's `translateX` offset. The mask handles the visual clipping. ## Scroll Behavior The portal has three scroll phases. Parallax is driven by `transform: translateY()` on the inner color blend div, animated via the Web Animations API with a `ScrollTimeline`. ### Phase 1: Normal Scroll (before portal) When the portal top is **below** the viewport top, the portal scrolls normally with the content with no additional effects. The inner div's `translateY` is `0` — the image moves with the container at 1× scroll speed. ### Phase 2: Parallax (inside portal) The user is "inside the portal" when the portal fills the screen — its top edge has scrolled above the viewport top and its bottom edge is still below the viewport bottom. During this phase, the inner div's `translateY` increases gradually, shifting the image down within the portal container. The outer container (mask) continues scrolling at 1×, so the mask acts as a sliding window over the slower-moving image. - **Parallax starts** when the portal's top edge reaches the viewport's top edge. - **Parallax ends** when the portal's bottom edge reaches the viewport's **bottom** edge — the moment normal content starts appearing below the portal. ### Phase 3: Normal Scroll (after portal) Once the user has scrolled past the portal (normal content is visible below), `translateY` holds at its final value and stops incrementing. The portal resumes scrolling at 1× with the content. The parallax effect is only active while the user is "inside" the portal. ### Parallax shift The total parallax displacement scales with the portal's height: ``` PARALLAX_SHIFT = portalHeight * (1 - PARALLAX_RATE) ``` where `PARALLAX_RATE` is the ratio of the image's scroll speed to the container's scroll speed (e.g. `PARALLAX_RATE = 0.5` means the image moves at half the speed of the mask, producing a shift of `portalHeight * 0.5`). ### Small portals (portal shorter than viewport) If the portal's total height is less than the viewport height, no parallax phase occurs. `endFraction` clamps to `startFraction` via `Math.max`, producing a zero-length parallax range. This is intentional — if the portal fits entirely on screen there is no "scrolling through" it, so parallax doesn't apply. ### Implementation Parallax is implemented via the Web Animations API with `ScrollTimeline`, which runs on the compositor — no JavaScript on the scroll path. The animation keyframes use dynamic offsets computed from the portal's position. `scrollableHeight` is `document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight`. - `startFraction = portalDocumentY / scrollableHeight` - `endFraction = max(startFraction, (portalDocumentY + portalHeight - viewportHeight) / scrollableHeight)` ```js element.animate([ { offset: 0, transform: 'translateY(0px)' }, { offset: startFraction, transform: 'translateY(0px)' }, { offset: endFraction, transform: `translateY(${PARALLAX_SHIFT}px)` }, { offset: 1, transform: `translateY(${PARALLAX_SHIFT}px)` }, ], { timeline: new ScrollTimeline({ source: document.documentElement }), fill: 'both' }) ``` --- ## Multiple Portals Multiple portals can coexist on-screen (e.g. two thoughts with context view active simultaneously). Each context view activation produces its own set of `showContexts` children in the linearized tree. To support this: 1. Group portal children by their parent path. 2. Render one portal `
` per group. 3. Each portal computes its own bounding box, parallax offset, and mask independently. --- ## Element Structure ```
← Outer: portal container (position, mask, stacking)
← Inner: color blend (image, transform for parallax + autofocus)
``` ### Outer div (portal container) | Property | Value | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `position` | `absolute` | Positioned within LayoutTree's inner container | | `top` | Bounding box of portal parent + children | Tracks portal region vertically | | `left` | `-50vw` | Extends past left edge of viewport | | `width` | `200vw` | Ensures full horizontal coverage | | `height` | Bounding box + vertical padding | Covers all portal thoughts with mask breathing room | | `z-index` | `-1` | Behind thought text | | `pointer-events` | `none` | Non-interactive | | `overflow` | `hidden` | Clips the inner image to the portal region | | `mask-image` | `mask-composite` (match reference image) | Feathered vignette mask | | `transition` | `top 150ms, height 150ms` | Smooth resize when portal bounds change | ### Inner div (color blend) | Property | Value | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `width` | `100%` | Fills the portal container | | `height` | `max(portalHeight, 1.5 × viewportHeight)` | Oversized for parallax headroom | | `background-image` | portal.avif | The spectral hue effect | | `background-size` | `cover` | Fill the inner div | | `background-position-x` | `bgOffsetX` | Autofocus horizontal shift | | `transform` | `translateY(parallaxOffset)` | Parallax vertical shift (compositor-driven via ScrollTimeline) | | `transition` | `background-position-x 750ms ease-out` | Smooth autofocus animation; Y is driven by ScrollTimeline, not CSS transitions |
input.title: "Portal" system for transcluded views

input.body:
## Goal

Automatically assign an existing GitHub milestone to each new issue when it is created.

The milestone should be selected by GitHub Models inference using repository-owned instructions, samples, and the current list of open GitHub milestones.

This workflow should have a similar structure to the Everhour estimate generator, but the write target is GitHub issue metadata rather than Everhour.

## Core Behavior

On new issue creation:

1. Trigger on `issues.opened`.
2. Skip if the issue already has a milestone.
3. Fetch the current list of open milestones from GitHub.
4. Load milestone inference instructions.
5. Load milestone samples.
6. Call GitHub Models to choose the best milestone.
7. Validate the output.
8. Assign the selected milestone to the issue.
9. Do not comment on success.

Success should be quiet. The assigned milestone is sufficient.

## Repository Structure

```txt
.github/
  workflows/
    assign-issue-milestone.yml

  instructions/
    milestone/
      milestone.instructions.md
      milestones.json
      samples/
        issue-123.json
```

## Milestone Instructions

`milestone.instructions.md` should contain:

- milestone selection policy
- how to interpret issue titles, bodies, and labels
- how to use available milestone metadata
- ambiguity handling
- confidence policy
- strict output format requirements

The model must only select from the provided open milestones.

It must not invent milestones.

It must not select closed milestones.

It must not use a fallback or generic backlog milestone.

## Open Milestones Only

The workflow should fetch only open milestones from GitHub.

Closed milestones should not be included in the model prompt.

If there are no open milestones, the workflow should fail and leave a comment explaining that no milestone was assigned because there are no open milestones.

## Rename Resilience

The workflow should be resilient to GitHub milestone renaming.

Samples should not depend directly on GitHub milestone titles as permanent identifiers.

Use a repo-owned milestone mapping file:

```json
[
  {
    "id": "v-next",
    "githubTitle": "Next Release"
  },
  {
    "id": "ux-polish",
    "githubTitle": "UX Polish"
  }
]
```

The model should output the stable repo-owned milestone `id`, not the GitHub milestone title.

At runtime:

1. Load `milestones.json`.
2. Fetch current open GitHub milestones.
3. Resolve selected stable `id` to `githubTitle`.
4. Resolve `githubTitle` to the current GitHub milestone number.
5. Update the issue using the milestone number.

If a GitHub milestone is renamed, update `milestones.json` rather than rewriting samples.

## Model Output Schema

The model should return only JSON:

```json
{
  "milestone": "ux-polish",
  "confidence": "high"
}
```

Valid confidence values:

```txt
low
medium
high
```

Only `high` confidence should result in automatic assignment.

Policy:

```txt
confidence = high   → assign milestone
confidence = medium → fail and comment
confidence = low    → fail and comment
```

## Low Confidence Behavior

There should be no fallback milestone.

If confidence is not `high`, the workflow should:

1. Assign no milestone.
2. Leave a comment explaining that milestone inference failed.
3. Fail the workflow.

Example comment:

```md
Milestone inference failed.

Reason: Low confidence selecting an existing open milestone.

No milestone was assigned.
```

## Validation

The workflow should validate that:

- model output is valid JSON
- output contains a valid stable milestone id
- confidence is one of `low`, `medium`, or `high`
- selected milestone id exists in `milestones.json`
- selected milestone resolves to a currently open GitHub milestone
- confidence is `high` before assignment

If validation fails, the workflow should fail and comment.

Do not assign a milestone when validation fails.

## Sample Format

Each sample should contain issue input and expected milestone id.

```json
{
  "input": {
    "title": "Bug title",
    "body": "Structured issue body markdown",
    "labels": ["bug", "frontend"]
  },
  "expected": {
    "milestone": "ux-polish"
  }
}
```

Manual correction samples can include provenance later if a correction workflow is added.

## Workflow YAML Shape

```yaml
name: Assign issue milestone

on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: write

jobs:
  assign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - run: yarn install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Assign milestone
        run: yarn milestone:assign
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

## Package Script

Add a package script:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "milestone:assign": "tsx scripts/assign-issue-milestone.ts"
  }
}
```

## Suggested TypeScript Structure

Exact paths can be adjusted to match repo conventions.

```txt
scripts/
  assign-issue-milestone.ts

src/
  inference/
    callGitHubModel.ts
    validateJson.ts

  milestone/
    assignIssueMilestone.ts
    buildMilestonePrompt.ts
    loadMilestoneInstructions.ts
    loadMilestoneSamples.ts
    loadMilestoneMap.ts
    listOpenMilestones.ts
    resolveMilestone.ts
    validateMilestoneSelection.ts
```

## Inference Inputs

The model prompt should include:

- issue title
- issue body
- issue labels
- current open milestone list
- stable milestone ids from `milestones.json`
- milestone descriptions, if useful
- milestone samples
- strict output schema

The model should not be allowed to choose outside the supplied milestone ids.

## Retry Policy

Retry model inference up to three times on invalid output.

Invalid output includes:

- malformed JSON
- missing fields
- unknown milestone id
- invalid confidence value
- selected milestone does not resolve to an open GitHub milestone

After three failed attempts:

1. Assign no milestone.
2. Comment with failure reason.
3. Fail the workflow.

Do not apply a fallback milestone.

## Success Behavior

On success:

input.body:
## Background

`formatSelection` currently applies formatting (bold, italic, strikethrough, underline, code, foreColor, backColor, removeFormat) via `document.execCommand`. Because `execCommand` mutates the contentEditable DOM directly, the resulting state change only re-enters Redux later via the contentEditable's `onChange` → debounced `thoughtChangeHandler` → `editThought`. This introduces an **async gap** between the command and the resulting `editThought` dispatch.

This async gap is the root cause of a whole class of undo/redo complexity:

- Applying foreground + background color is two separate dispatches that must be stitched into a single undo step.
- The follow-up cleanup pass (strip default bg/fg, unwrap empty `font`/`span` tags) is a *second* dispatch that also must merge.
- To stitch these together across the async gap, we built the entire `batchEditing` apparatus: `batchEditing.ts`, `mergePrev` / `MergePrevActionPayload`, the `edited` flag, a deferred `setTimeout`-based batch close (to survive the async gap on mobile WebViews), and wiring in `Editable.tsx`, `Note.tsx`, and `formatSelection.ts`.

See #4628 (interim fix) and #4620 for the undo bug this complexity works around.

## Proposal

Reimplement `formatSelection` to compute the new HTML **synchronously** using `DOMParser` (which we already use for the background-color/tag-cleanup pass) and dispatch a **single** `editThought` / `setDescendant`. With formatting applied in one synchronous dispatch:

- foreColor + backColor land in a single dispatch → a single undo step with no stitching.
- The cleanup pass merges into the same synchronous transform instead of being a second dispatch.
- There is no async gap, so **no batching is needed at all**.

This lets us delete:

- `src/stores/batchEditing.ts`
- `src/@types/MergePrevActionPayload.ts`
- `mergePrev` wiring in `src/components/Editable.tsx`, `src/components/Note.tsx`, and `src/actions/formatSelection.ts`
- The `mergePrev` handling in `undoRedoEnhancer` (restoring it to a fully action-type-agnostic, patch-based undo system)

## Design constraint

`undoRedoEnhancer` must remain a generalized, patch-based undo/redo system that works on any Redux state patch. It must **not** become aware of formatting-specific action types. Removing `mergePrev` entirely (rather than deriving it centrally) satisfies this.

## Subtleties / acceptance criteria

The rewrite must preserve current behavior, including the parts where `execCommand` is doing non-trivial work:

- [ ] **Partial-selection formatting.** Formatting applied to an arbitrary sub-range of a thought (e.g. bold on a few characters mid-word, color on a selected word) must correctly split text nodes, wrap the exact range, and merge adjacent identical spans — including nested (`<b><i>`) and overlapping ranges. This is the hardest case; the whole-thought path is straightforward.
- [ ] **Selection/caret restoration.** After replacing `innerHTML` via a synchronous `editThought`, the caret/selection must be restored to the correct offset for both whole-thought and partial-selection cases. Existing machinery (`selection.offsetThought()`, `savedSelection`) can be reused but must cover the partial-range case.
- [ ] **All commands.** Handle `bold | italic | strikethrough | underline | code | removeFormat` in addition to color, including toggle on/off based on current formatting state (equivalent to `queryCommandState`).
- [ ] **Note vs. thought.** Preserve the note-vs-thought branching (`setDescendant` vs `editThought`) and note-specific default colors (`fgNote`).
- [ ] **Mobile behavior.** Preserve the mobile edit-mode selection/keyboard behavior (#3996) — no async gap means the `setTimeout` deferral in `endBatchEditing` is no longer needed.
- [ ] Regression tests in `src/commands/__tests__/undo-redo.ts` and `e2e/puppeteer/__tests__/undo.ts` continue to pass (a single undo reverts only the most recent color application).

## Sequencing

This is a follow-up to #4628, which lands an interim fix for the undo bug. This issue tracks the root-cause migration that makes the batching apparatus unnecessary.
input.title: Migrate formatSelection off document.execCommand to a synchronous DOMParser-based transform

Moved over from #4657 

When a thought is deleted (using backspace, the delete toolbar button, or app-level undo) then any undo steps associated with the removed DOM element are orphaned. They still appear in the native undo stack, but native undo tries to make edits that have no valid target and do nothing.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create thought 'One'
2. Create thought 'Two'
3. Click Delete toolbar button
4. Shake
5. Tap Undo on native dialog

## Expected behavior

'Two' should be re-created

## Current behavior

Nothing happens. When shaking again, Undo and Redo are both available because iOS has modified its native undo stack.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/69bcbac7-95af-4746-af98-9fe4c3710869

---

Shaking to undo a second time does re-create 'Two' because the second undo step in iOS's native stack points to 'One'. This allows the app to intercept a `beforeinput` event and redirect native undo functionality to app-level undo.

## Intercepting native undo events using `beforeinput`

Using an event handler to intercept `beforeinput` events solves related inconsistencies with native undo behavior. Calling `preventDefault` on native undo and allowing app-level undo to run instead means that it works the same as Ctrl-Z or the toolbar buttons, and gives us full control over undo behavior. The only thing that we don't have control over is WebKit's native undo stack.

Without the `beforeinput` handler, native undo works differently from app-level undo. It will not delete a thought on its own, which means that this issue occurs less frequently. However, following the repro steps above will result in a bug whether native undo is intercepted or not. In fact, native undo is *not* intercepted in this case, because the `beforeinput` event cannot be captured when it is orphaned (sent to an element that no longer exists) and so native undo runs but does nothing.

---

## Previous attempt (high effort + low impact)

**Solution:** Create a dummy editable that can have `execCommand` called on it to create a new (duplicate) undo step.

**Rationale:** If a deleted thought orphans a native undo step, then a follow-up command can be run on a dummy editable that is always guaranteed to exist.

**Trade-offs:**

- need to create and manage focus on a dummy editable
- possibly need to create a middleware to detect thought deletion (I didn't go too deep on this because I didn't see it fully fixing the problem)
- need to call `execCommand('undo')` a second time to try to skip the orphaned step when it sees that the dummy editable is the target of an undo step

**Verdict:** This doesn't truly solve the problem, and the native undo stack ends up with orphaned steps somewhere inside of it. So it's probably not worth it for the following reasons:

- Trying to skip an orphaned undo step may work in the undo direction, but will not work in the redo direction because the orphaned step is invoked before the follow-up correcting step.
- The assumption that the last native undo step will target the deleted editable doesn't always hold, such as editing one thought immediately before deleting a different thought. The `deleteThought` action doesn't actually create an undo step, so it's kind of guesswork to decide to add an `execCommand` undo step on the dummy editable at that point.

Here is a video showing how an orphaned undo step can end up in the middle of the stack rather than in a more predictable place at the end of the stack:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c29962dd-4e5e-4c66-9f69-e343538f2f9e
input.title: [iOS] Deleting a thought creates an orphaned native undo step

## Problem

We have ~64 open pull requests at the moment, which is quite the backlog.
* As a developer, it is difficult to filter for PRs that need additional work.
* As a reviewer, it is difficult to filter for PRs that require a (re-)review.
* As a maintainer, it is difficult to filter for PRs that are ready to merge.
* As the **em** project, many PRs that would improve me get lost in limbo.

GitHub notifications are probably the best way to find PRs requiring an individual's attention at the moment, but notifications are noisy and somewhat lossy (opened -> marked as read -> defer until later -> lost in limbo).

We currently have labels for categorization, e.g. `bug`, `feature`, `dependencies`, `hold`. However, these are only being used by ~10 of ~64 PRs.

## Proposal

We should add the following labels:

| Label Name | Color | Assignee | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Status: Draft` | 🟨 | Developer | The developer is still working on the PR. |
| `Status: In Review` | 🟦 | Reviewer | The developer believes the PR is ready to merge, pending review. |
| `Status: Changes Requested` | 🟥 | Developer | The reviewer identified changes that should be made by the developer. |
| `Status: Ready to Merge` | 🟩 | Maintainer (@raineorshine) | The PR has been approved by the reviewer and is ready to merge. |

And follow this workflow:
* **(1) Developer creates an initial PR**
  * Developer assigns it to themself (the developer)
  * Developer sets the label to `Status: Draft`
* **(2) Developer finishes the PR**
  * Developer assigns it to the reviewer
  * Developer sets the label to `Status: In Review`
* **(3) Reviewer finishes their PR review**
  * If changes requested
    * Reviewer assigns it back to the developer
    * Reviewer sets the label to `Status: Changes Requested`
    * Return to (2) until the developer finishes the requested changes
  * If approved
    * Reviewer assigns it to @raineorshine 
    * Reviewer sets the label to `Status: Ready to Merge`
* **(4) Maintainer merges the PR**

With this system:
* As a developer, I can filter for all PRs assigned to me with `Status: Draft` or `Status: Changes Requested` to easily see a list of PRs needing my attention.
* As a reviewer, I can filter for all PRs assigned to me with `Status: In Review` to easily see a list of PRs requiring my review.
* As a maintainer, I can filter for all PRs assigned to me with `Status: Ready to Merge` to easily see a list of PRs ready for me to verify and merge.
* As the **em** project, it brings me great joy to see PRs systematically progressing towards my own improvement.

### Cost

This does require a small overhead for contributors to keep the assignees and labels of PRs up-to-date, but is almost certainly worth the benefits.

### Automation

We could potentially use an LLM agent to read a PR's comments, CI checks, etc. and attempt to set the label and assignee automatically if it's out of sync with the actual status of the pull request. I believe keeping them up-to-date manually is very reasonable, however, as it's extremely simple to do and likely beneficial for contributors to be conscious of when/why a PR is moved through the stages.

It would make sense for our developer agents to follow the workflow of the developer, e.g.
* Setting `Status: In Review` and assigning the reviewer after completing a PR
* Responding to PRs that have been reassigned and marked with `Status: Changes Requested`
